Well that's depressing. It's getting harder and harder to be over-the-top paranoid these days.

I've been becoming increasingly "paranoid* about data security over the years. I don't do anything illegal, but it's still my stuff to share or not. I guess the big question this brings up is how can we get rid of this software? Replace the HD firmware?

Making replacement firmware is pretty much beyond the capabilities of anyone outside of the drive manufacturer. Even so, say Toshiba made replacement firmware available for their drives, who is to say that that firmware isn't also compromised and that it even installed successfully?

I certainly wouldn't trust one of the compromised manufacturers providing firmware replacements. I was thinking an open source solution would come along, though I admittedly know nothing about what it takes for the firmware to make a HD work.

What the NSA (seems very likely they're behind this) has done is really, really bad.

There are only a few companies with the facilities necessary to make magnetic hard drives, the chances of open source firmware being made available are practically nil.

For SSD drives .. who knows? Even so, the controller chips are still only made by a few companies but it least it would be an issue of making a new controller chip and using off the shelf NAND which seems a little more feasible.

I'm no expert though.

In my ignorance I'm comparing the firmware on hard drives to a router's firmware. From what you're saying here, it looks like that is a faulty comparison. It would seem that the firmware on the router is, by nature, accessible to the end user for upgrades, which opens it up to having a 3rd party firmware put on it.

Hard drives, on the other hand, don't have a known avenue to (easily) access the firmware for any sort of modification. I've worked with some non-PC technology down to the component level, so I know that barring a physical write protect anything can be rewritten if you know how. If I understand you correctly the firmware on HDs is either physically protected, or requires specialized equipment that most people won't have access to. Does that sound about right?

I'm not sure exactly how you'd unlock HD firmware so it can be written to. Obviously, it can be done though. Thanks so the NSA, hackers are going to be very interested in this. Imagine planting this stuff on servers used for banking. You could gradually suck millions out of the international banking industry without detection. Even if the NSA acted with honest intentions in developing exploits like this, in the long game, they've hurt everybody and made their jobs much harder. Some people need to go to jail for making this terrible call.

I think two-factor authentication for pretty much everything just become a big priority. They may be able to hack the accounts and see the information, but if the ability to do anything with it was tied to some form of multi-factor authentication their trespass should be stopped there.

However, your assessment of what hackers will now want to do brings up a tricky question regarding state secrets. Has the public at large been done a service with this information coming to light. Certainly it may well have been a matter of time before infecting the firmware on HDs or other components of computers became a thing, but did the release of this story just shorten the timetable on this?

Well, I guess it's time to strap on my tinfoil hat and start saving all of my sensitive data on an internal network with absolutely no internet access and encrypting the ever living daylights out of it. Unless they can hack it through a power cable they'll be SOL.

I guess it's one thing as a hacker or malware coder to sit and idly wonder if something like this could ever be pulled off, and another thing to know that not only is it possible - it's already been done.

Exactly. Before they had to wonder if it was even worth the effort of trying to figure out. Now they not only know it works, but they know that it's virtually undetectable and will survive even disc formats.

I'm a little curious - I think I know what you mean by the "Analog Backlash", but could you elaborate on it a little? If only to hear a little more on your opinion on this topic.

Sure!

The analog backlash refers to the trending/inevitable move against digital technology. There are two key factors. One is basic trendwatching - tech like the first ipod nano was very cool circa 2006. This is what made technology non-"nerdy" and mass acceptable. What followed was an acceptance of being attached to facebook, chatting, etc. Prior to this it was still very uncool to live most of your life with/via technology. The natural life cycle of trends has now played out - everyone's grandma and baby niece has an ipad and there's really nothing life-changing coming out of tech these days. It's no longer cool. What is becoming the new cool marker within the next few years is the ability to avoid tech. To be above it, but more importantly to not NEED it. If you have real friends you don't need instagram followers and shit like that. This will steamroll.

Far more interesting is the real version. This depends on age and generations. For Baby Boomers and Gen X technology (the internet etc) came into their lives reasonably late. It starts around 1994, so people who were teenagers or older in those years remember a different world where you memorized phone numbers, nobody had email, and you read actual newspapers to get news. So technology was seen as a force of change and it was embraced/etc with that in mind.

For the first wave of your millenials, who were like 5-12 when this stuff came out it was a status signifier. Having it was the provenance of those with reasonable income and knowing the hot new thing carried some currency. These are the instagram-embracing people who have always grown up with this shallow attitude of demonstrating/personal branding. They are the ultimate consumers of technology and irritate everyone else.

So what happened after them? The next generation grew up with technology always existing. There is nothing novel to an 18 year-old about the internet and its assorted technologies - they have literally always existed. And they see their slightly older siblings obsessed with Instagram, and the boomer types buying ipads and waxing about the "impact of technology" in ways they simply cannot relate to at all. Their reaction is predictable - a move away from tech. It also helps that they are broke so it is not seen as desirable to blow all your money on a fancy gadget - that's seen as stupid consumerism. These are the people for whom taking a 30-day break from facebook/etc is a novel idea. And they love it.

The reason is that the "analog" experiences that older people had are NOVEL to them. Going into nature without a cell phone, not being able to be reached for weeks at a time via electronic messages, etc, is a new experience. And it's super relaxing! It sets them apart when they "discover" this way to live and it's already becoming a differentiator. Those who are brave enough to choose this approach demonstrate a confidence and natural way of being that is more attractive than the instagram tart, etc. Eventually as they turn this into the next big thing the older generations will copy them so they can be like "young people." You know the rest.

As always, the kids will save us.
